integrated_multimodal_description:
vertical 9:16 cinematic composition, with thin black widescreen letterbox bars at top and bottom giving a 2.39:1 film aspect inside the vertical frame. FULL COLOUR, NOT black-and-white, NOT monochrome, NOT desaturated — a richly coloured 1850s period film with a classic TEAL-AND-ORANGE colour grade: warm orange skin tones, amber lamplight and golden-orange prairie light in the highlights; deep teal-cyan shadows pooling in the carriage corners, beneath the carriages and along the shaded side of the train; the sky carrying a cool teal-blue tint against warm cream clouds; mahogany interiors reading warm orange-brown against muted teal-green velvet. Soft naturalistic film grain throughout. A montage-style contemplative rail-journey short, edited as five intercut shots that build from the crowded carriage to the open prairie and back in to the man. Pacing is measured and unhurried, each cut landing on a clear beat of the train's rhythm.

LOOK (the young man from <Picture 1>, in every shot, never deviating): pale skin with realistic pore-level texture, high sharp cheekbones, a clean angular jawline, a long straight nose, light cool-blue-grey eyes, soft natural pink lips, soft blonde wavy tousled hair of medium length that the wind keeps lifting at the crown. Outfit: a high-collared cream silk shirt with fine lace ruffle down the front placket, worn under a deep-burgundy velvet waistcoat with a double row of ornate gold filigree buttons and gold braid trim along the lapels and armholes. Restrained 1850s European aristocratic; no jewellery, the shirt collar open one button at the throat.

SPATIAL RULES (consistent across all shots — the geography must hold together):
The steam locomotive pulls the train toward screen-RIGHT; the prairie, blue sky and clouds are always on the screen-RIGHT side of the train. The compartment's interior corridor wall is screen-LEFT. The man always sits on the screen-RIGHT side of the compartment, facing screen-RIGHT toward the window. When he leans out of the window in Shot 04, ONLY his head and neck extend beyond the window frame — his shoulders, chest, torso and arms all remain fully inside the compartment; he is NOT climbing out of the window, NOT leaning his upper body out, just resting his head out naturally with one forearm laid on the window sill. The camera for Shot 04 is INSIDE the compartment, positioned DIRECTLY BEHIND the man (on the screen-LEFT corridor side of his seat), looking past the back of his head toward the open window — a pure from-behind angle: the frame shows ONLY the back of his head, his ears, the nape of his neck and his shoulders from behind, with the window view filling the space around his head — NEVER his face, NEVER his jawline, NEVER his cheek, NEVER a three-quarter or side view of his head, and the camera never drifts around toward his face at any point in that shot. Shot 03 is a wide exterior of the whole train, filmed from the prairie at a low angle on the screen-RIGHT side, the locomotive leading at screen-RIGHT with the carriages trailing back to screen-LEFT. Shot 05 is a low angle on the track itself — a SINGLE-TRACK rural prairie railway, just one single set of running rails on one single row of wooden sleepers, NOT a double-track mainline, NOT two parallel sets of tracks, just one lone line of rail cutting through grass on both sides: the train passes closest to camera and then continues away toward screen-RIGHT, so that once the locomotive has gone, the last thing the camera sees is the REAR of the train — the back of the final carriage — receding along that single line of track into the distance, never the locomotive coming toward camera.

WINDOW VIEW RULE (applies to Shots 01, 02 and 04 — this is critical):
Everything seen through his window is EMPTY, BEAUTIFUL, UNTOUCHED OPEN PRAIRIE — only golden grass, wildflowers, distant poplar trees, open sky and slow white clouds. Through his window there is NEVER another train, NEVER a passing locomotive, NEVER an oncoming train, NEVER a second train on a neighbouring track, NEVER any railway track or rails, NEVER a station, NEVER a bridge, NEVER any building, fence or road. There is exactly ONE train in this entire film — the one he is riding — and that train is only ever seen from OUTSIDE in Shots 03 and 05; it is NEVER visible from his own window.

[Shot 01 | 0.00s – 3.20s] MEDIUM CLOSE-UP, three-quarter rear-side view, eye-level, slight hand-held sway. NO full-body shot and NO wide shot of the carriage — the film opens already tight on <Picture 1> (the man), framed from a three-quarter angle behind his screen-LEFT shoulder: his face turned toward the screen-RIGHT window, his cheekbone and jawline catching the window light, his soft blonde wavy hair lifted gently at the crown, the lace of his collar just visible. The crowded 1850s first-class compartment lives only in the soft-focus background around him: an older grey-whiskered gentleman in a frock coat reading a folded newspaper opposite him; a mother in a bonnet with a small girl beside her; a travelling salesman in a bowler hat dozing with a carpet bag between his feet; mahogany panelling and worn green velvet seats melting into teal-shadowed bokeh; a brass luggage net overhead; a faint haze of coal smoke; an unlit brass oil-lamp swinging. Sunlight and shadow from the wide-open prairie sky flash in warm orange stripes across his shoulder and across the blurred passengers; through the window beyond him is only golden grass and open sky. He is simply watching the window, his light cool-blue-grey eyes fixed on the moving view, his breath slow.
Camera: hand-held medium close-up holding his three-quarter rear-side angle, focus locked on his face and the window light on his hair; the carriage is never shown in full wide and the man is never shown full-body — the composition stays tight on him from the start.

[Shot 02 | 3.20s – 6.00s] MEDIUM CLOSE-UP, profile, eye-level. Tighter on <Picture 1> (the man): his face in clean profile, his right shoulder leaned against the wooden window frame, his light cool-blue-grey eyes tracking the view outside. The window is down: through it, endless untouched prairie rolls past fast — sun-bleached golden grass bending in the wind, scattered wildflowers, a distant stand of poplars, an unbroken pale-blue sky with slow white cumulus, and nothing else at all: NO other train, NO locomotive, NO tracks, NO buildings, just pure empty beautiful open country. The slipstream lifts the soft wavy blonde hair at his crown, ruffles the lace at his throat and stirs the open collar of the cream silk shirt. The other passengers are reduced to blurred shapes in the foreground and background — the newspaper rustling, the child's voice. He blinks slowly once and a strand of hair blows across his forehead; he does not brush it away.
Camera: locked-off profile from the seat opposite, focus locked on his face; the window view is a soft horizontal motion-blur.

[Shot 03 | 6.00s – 8.50s] WIDE EXTERIOR, low angle, the montage cut-out. The whole steam train crossing the open prairie, seen from the grass at trackside on the screen-RIGHT side of the train: the black iron locomotive leading at screen-RIGHT with its tall chimney, cowcatcher and driving wheels with visible coupling rods pumping; behind it a long line of varnished timber carriages trailing back to screen-LEFT; a great plume of white steam and black coal smoke streaming from the chimney and flattening downwind over the grass; the carriages' small windows flashing sunlight. The train is moving fast toward screen-RIGHT and the camera holds still as it passes, the ground trembling slightly. Endless golden prairie and enormous sky all around, a distant windmill and a line of poplars on the horizon.
Camera: static low wide angle on the prairie, the train crossing frame left to right, slight heat-shimmer off the grass, no whip-pan — the power is in the train's own speed.

[Shot 04 | 8.50s – 12.00s] INTERIOR, MEDIUM CLOSE-UP FROM DIRECTLY BEHIND, over-the-shoulder-from-behind. The camera is INSIDE the compartment, positioned directly behind <Picture 1> (the man) at his back, looking over his shoulder toward the open window. He sits at the screen-RIGHT window seat and leans his head slightly out through the open window — his head just past the window frame edge, chin level with the sill, one forearm laid along the sill, shoulders, chest, torso and arms all kept fully inside the compartment; NOT climbing out, NOT leaning his upper body out. From directly behind, the frame holds ONLY the back of his head, his ears, the nape of his neck and his shoulders from behind — NO face, NO jawline, NO cheek, NO side profile, and the camera never drifts around toward his face. Around and beyond his head, the open window frames nothing but beautiful open prairie racing past — golden-orange grass bending in waves, scattered wildflowers, a distant line of poplars, cool teal-blue sky and slow cream clouds, and absolutely nothing else: NO other train, NO locomotive, NO oncoming train, NO rails, NO tracks, NO buildings — exactly the view he is watching, so the audience sees what he sees. The wind coming in through the window blows his soft blonde wavy hair BACK toward the camera, lifting and rippling it in slow waves, the lace at the back of his collar fluttering; the leather strap of the drop-sash window sways gently. As the shot opens, the locomotive up ahead sounds its whistle — he does not flinch; the back of his head stays still, quietly watching the view.
Camera: locked-off directly behind him inside the compartment, slight hand-held sway, the back of his head sharp in the foreground with the window view around and beyond it, the dim compartment interior in teal shadow at the frame edges.

[Shot 05 | 12.00s – 15.00s] EXTREME LOW ANGLE, track level, the montage close. The camera lies low on the ballast beside a SINGLE-TRACK rural prairie railway — just one single set of running rails on one single row of wooden sleepers, NOT a double-track mainline, NOT two parallel sets of tracks, just one lone line of rail with grass on both sides of the ballast. The train thunders past almost overhead: great iron driving wheels and pumping coupling rods filling the frame one by one, carriage wheels flashing, the single rail and its single row of sleepers blurring beneath, ballast stones flickering, steam venting down and billowing across the lens. As the last carriage sweeps past, the camera tilts up slowly — and what remains in frame is the REAR of the train: the varnished timber back of the final carriage with its small end window and brass fittings, shrinking away down that single straight line of track toward screen-RIGHT into the enormous golden prairie and open sky, a single thread of white steam and black smoke trailing along the line of it and thinning against the clouds. The clatter of the wheels fades with distance, the prairie wind returning underneath.
Camera: extreme low on the ballast for the pass, then a slow tilt up holding on the receding rear of the train, ending wide on the empty prairie as the final carriage disappears toward the horizon.

overall_soundscape:
ambient — LOUD, insistent, real train motion: the heavy rhythmic CLACK-CLACK-CLACK of iron wheels crossing rail joints, faster and more forceful than a modern train, the deep grinding rumble and groan of the timber carriage body, the whoosh of open prairie wind through the down window, the small wooden rattle of the drop-sash window in its frame, brass luggage net and couplings jingling
specific — the steady chuffing exhaust of the steam locomotive, the hiss and long slow release of the safety valve, the screech of flange metal on a curve, the conductor's distant call down the corridor, a newspaper turning, the small girl's voice in Shot 01, the squeak of leather seats
LOUD STEAM WHISTLE — at 8.60s, just after the cut to Shot 04, the locomotive sounds one long, loud, piercing steam whistle, two-note chording, that cuts through everything else in the mix for a full two seconds, reverberating off the open prairie; it decays slowly into the wind and leaves a ringing in the ear
emotional — open, hollow, airy prairie acoustics with a long tail on the whistle; the wind tone is noticeably wilder and louder once his head goes out the window in Shot 04

non_diegetic_music:
a gentle 1850s salon-music ensemble, period-appropriate and unhurried: a felt-hammer parlour piano playing a soft lilting waltz figure in 3/4 time in the manner of an early-Victorian salon waltz, key of G major, rubato and slightly nostalgic, accompanied by a small string trio — two violins and one cello — the cello holding long sustained roots while the violins weave a slow counter-melody around the piano; a Celtic harp answers the piano phrases sparsely. The ensemble enters quietly at 1.5s beneath the rhythm of the wheels and sounds as if heard from an adjacent parlour room — slightly distant, warm, full, alive. It drops out entirely to let the steam whistle stand alone at 8.60s, then returns fuller and warmer over the track-level pass and the receding train in Shot 05, the piano melody blooming into one long sustained chord with the strings as the camera tilts up onto the rear of the disappearing train, fading out slowly into the prairie wind. No percussion, no modern instruments, no drums, no guitar, no synth.

这个串法是在做 sigma 调度拆分 + 分段采样，常见于 ComfyUI 里一些分阶段采样的工作流（比如 H3 视频生成、teaser 采样器之类）。 串起来后数据流是这样的： 
1.  基础调度器
生成一个 10 步的 beta 调度 sigma 曲线，从最高噪声一路降到 0。 
2.  H3 Sigma Refiner
接管上面的 sigma 序列，在 sigma 0.70 → 0.00 这段区间里额外插入 1 步细化（cosine 分布）。
也就是说，原先 10 步的序列，在这个低噪声区间会被“加密”，总步数会变多。  
3.  分离Sigmas
把 Refiner 处理后的完整 sigma 序列，按 步数 4 切成两段： • high_sigmas：前 4 步，对应高噪声阶段（粗生成） • low_sigmas：后面剩下的步数，对应低噪声阶段（细化和收尾）   
 通俗理解：
你先让 H3 Sigma Refiner 把“收尾那段”的步数加密，然后 Split Sigmas 一刀把全过程砍成「前期粗画」和「后期精修」两部分，方便接给两个不同的采样器或者分阶段控制。
